newsitem.title: FRANCE: FRENCH ELECTION - HOW THEY VOTE.
newsitem.headline: FRENCH ELECTION - HOW THEY VOTE.

text.p: French President Jacques Chirac dissolved the National Assembly on April 21 and called a snap parliamenty election, 10 months ahead of schedule, for May 25 and June 1.
Article 12 of the 1958 Fifth Republic constitution gives the president the right to dissolve the Assembly after consultations with the prime minister and the speakers of both houses of parliament.
A general election must be held 20 to 40 days after a decree is published in the Official Journal dissolving the Assembly.
The president may not dissolve parliament again in the first year of a new legislature.
The upper house, the Senate, is elected indirectly by local officials and is not affected by a dissolution of the Assembly.
Voting for the parliamentary election is held in two rounds in 577 single-member constituencies.
A candidate who wins more than 50 percent of votes cast on the first ballot is elected without a runoff.

Otherwise, any candidate who polls 12.5 percent of the number of registered voters may contest the second ballot. The candidate who wins the most votes on the runoff is elected, even if he or she does not poll 50 percent.
There are 555 constituencies in metropolitan France and 22 in overseas departments and territories.
Voting takes place on Sundays from 8 a.m. (0600 GMT) to 6 p.m. (1600 GMT) in most areas and 8 p.m. (1800 GMT) in Paris and major provincial citites.

No results, projections or exit polls may be published until the last polling stations have closed in metropolitan France. By law, no opinion polls may be published in the last week before the first round or between the two rounds.
On election night, television stations broadcast generally reliable projections of the outcome in votes cast and seats as soon as the last polls close at 8 p.m. (1800 GMT).

The parties are allotted equal time for election broadcasts on public radio and television between May 5 and 23. Campaign spending and individual donations to parties are limited by law. The parties also receive public funds proportionate to the number of votes they poll.
The last parliamentary election took place in March 1993. The state of the parties in the outgoing Assembly was:
RPR-UDF centre-right coalition 464
Socialist party and allies 61
Communist party and allies 24
Other left 14
Other right 13
Vacant seat 1
